blocks.text: Farmers have sold here since 1907; voters saved it from demolition.

Pike Place Market is a public market spread down a steep bluff above Elliott Bay on the western edge of downtown Seattle. It is among the older public farmers' markets in the country to have run without a break, and it is the city's most visited attraction, drawing more than 20 million people a year. Its founding idea, still in force, is "Meet the Producer": farmers and craftspeople rent tables by the day and sell what they themselves grow or make. Nearly 500 people also live in the Market's buildings, and a public authority runs the place with a charter to protect small businesses and serve low-income residents.

City councilman Thomas Revelle pushed through the ordinance that created the market. On opening day in August 1907 a handful of farmers pulled their wagons onto Pike Place and sold out by lunchtime. The first building went up that November, and by 1922 the layout looked much as it does now. In the 1960s a plan to tear the market down for a redevelopment called Pike Plaza ran into a citizens' campaign led by architect Victor Steinbrueck and the Friends of the Market. A 1971 ballot initiative created a historic preservation zone and put the market back in public hands.

The upper street level holds fishmongers, produce stands, flower sellers (many of them Hmong farmers) and craft tables under the covered arcades. The levels below hold antique dealers, comic and collectible shops, small family restaurants and one of Seattle's oldest head shops. Street performers work the market too, and the historic district has more than 30 international eateries. The Athenian Inn has been serving since 1909.
Explore the lower levels beneath the main arcade, where the antique, collectible and specialty shops are.
Look for the crafts on the Desimone Bridge and at the north end of the arcade toward Virginia Street, where craftspeople get first claim on the tables.
A 1962 World's Fair vision of the future, with a revolving glass floor.

The Space Needle is the observation tower that stands for Seattle, built for the 1962 World's Fair at what is now Seattle Center in Lower Queen Anne. At 605 feet it was briefly the tallest structure west of the Mississippi; downtown towers have since outgrown it, but none has replaced it as the city's emblem. Elevators lift you about 520 feet in roughly 41 seconds to a deck with views over the downtown skyline, Elliott Bay and the islands of Puget Sound, and on clear days to the Olympics, the Cascades, Mount Rainier and Mount Baker.

The design was a compromise. Fair chairman Edward Carlson, inspired by Stuttgart's TV tower, sketched a tethered balloon on a napkin; architect John Graham contributed the flying-saucer top; Victor Steinbrueck gave it the hourglass waist and tripod legs. Privately financed and squeezed onto a small lot that once held a fire station, it went up in under a year, with the last elevator car installed the day before the fair opened. Built to withstand 200 mph winds and a magnitude 9 earthquake, it was named the city's youngest landmark in 1999.

A 2017–2018 renovation replaced the old restaurant level with the Loupe, a glass floor that revolves once every 45 minutes so the city turns slowly beneath your feet. The open-air deck above now has floor-to-ceiling glass panels and glass benches you can lean back against, plus a café and bar. Between the two levels, the Oculus Stairs look down through a glass oculus onto the elevators running up and down the shaft.
Stay on the Loupe for a full 45-minute rotation to see the whole city pass beneath the glass floor.
At the foot of the Oculus Stairs, look down through the glass to watch the elevators climbing the core.
A 100-foot ceiling of blown glass glowing red beside the Space Needle.

This museum at Seattle Center is given over entirely to the studio glass of Dale Chihuly, the artist most responsible for turning blown glass into large-scale sculpture. It opened in May 2012 directly beside the Space Needle, on ground once occupied by the Fun Forest amusement park. The building, designed with architect Owen Richards, earned LEED silver certification. The museum also hosts Refract, a free festival of glass art from around Puget Sound, and has given thousands of free visits to Seattle public school students.

The visit moves through three parts. The galleries trace more than four decades of Chihuly's experiments with color, form and light, room by room: a Sealife Room, a Persian Ceiling of stacked glass seen from below, Mille Fiori, Ikebana and Float Boats, Chandeliers and a Macchia Forest. Next comes the Glasshouse, filled by a single suspended sculpture about 100 feet long in reds, oranges and yellows, one of the largest he has made. Outside, the garden pairs his glass with trees, plants and flowers chosen to set it off. A small theater shows short films of Chihuly's process and installations around the world, and in the Hot Shop local artists gather molten glass from the furnace and shape it while you watch. The bar displays more than 25 of Chihuly's personal collections.
Watch a Hot Shop glassblowing demonstration to see how pieces like those in the galleries are made.
For an overview of the whole garden and Glasshouse, look down on it from the Space Needle next door.
Walk the sidewalks Seattle buried when it raised its streets.

Beneath the sidewalks of Pioneer Square lies a warren of old basements, former sidewalks and areaways that once sat at street level. They exist because, after the Great Seattle Fire of June 1889 wiped out much of the wooden business district and waterfront, the city rebuilt in masonry and took the chance to fix chronic drainage problems and awkward grades on the low, tide-flat ground by Elliott Bay. Streets were raised by anywhere from a few feet to a full story.

Rather than burying everything, builders put up retaining walls along the new roadways and filled between them, leaving open gaps under the sidewalks next to the buildings. For a time pedestrians climbed ladders between the raised street and the old shopfronts; brick arches and glass vault lights eventually roofed over the gaps. Owners expected the original ground floors to end up below grade, so they kept them plain and saved the ornament for the floor above. Shoppers kept using the lower sidewalks until 1907, when the city condemned the Underground over plague fears. The spaces then fell into decay or served as storage, and reputedly as flophouses, gambling rooms, speakeasies and opium dens.

Only a small part has been made safe, and it can be seen only on guided tours. Bill Speidel's Underground Tour, running since 1965, starts from the Pioneer Building and passes disused storefronts, artifacts and tunnel entrances. Beneath the Streets, founded in 2013, covers other sections and runs themed tours, including one on the city's LGBTQ+ history.
From below, look up at the vault lights, small glass panes once clear and now amethyst-tinted, set into the sidewalk overhead.
Compare the bare original ground-floor facades with the decorated storeys above them.
Watch kayaks, trawlers and salmon climb between lake and sea.

Also called the Ballard Locks, this Army Corps of Engineers complex sits at the west end of Salmon Bay, between the Ballard and Magnolia neighborhoods. It joins the freshwater Lake Washington Ship Canal to the saltwater of Puget Sound and handles more boat traffic than any other lock in the country. Kayaks, pleasure boats, cargo ships and fishing boats back from the Bering Sea are raised or lowered as much as 26 feet in a matter of minutes. The locks, the fish ladder and the surrounding Carl S. English Jr. Botanical Gardens draw more than a million visitors a year.

Seattleites talked about a lake-to-sound canal from the 1850s, but construction only got going in 1911, after lawsuits from Ballard mill owners and lakeside landowners. The locks opened in 1917 and remade the region. Lake Washington dropped about nine feet, which stranded piers, dried out more than a thousand acres of wetland and killed off the Black River. Rivers were rerouted, and the salmon runs that use the locks today were partly introduced to make up for the runs that were lost. The complex is on the National Register of Historic Places and is a National Historic Civil Engineering Landmark.

There are two chambers to watch, a small one and a large one, plus a spillway dam and a visitors center. The fish ladder is unusual because it sits where salt water meets fresh. It was rebuilt in 1976 with 21 steps and an underground room where windows let you watch Chinook, coho and sockeye salmon working their way upstream. Recordings of Seattle poet Judith Roche's five-poem "Salmon Suite" accompany the view.
For the most salmon at the viewing windows, come between early July and mid-August.
Each lock chamber is drained for about two weeks a year, the large one usually in November and the small one in March, so you may find one empty.
Gehry's crumpled-guitar building, with the monorail running straight through it.

MOPOP is a nonprofit museum of contemporary popular culture at Seattle Center, next to the Space Needle. Microsoft co-founder Paul Allen opened it in 2000 as the Experience Music Project; a science fiction museum was folded in later, and the current name dates from 2016. Its holdings run past 80,000 artifacts, from Dorothy's dress to the largest collection of Jimi Hendrix material anywhere: handwritten lyrics, his own instruments and original photographs.

The building is as much the attraction as anything inside. Frank Gehry worked from photos and bodies of Fender Stratocasters, and the result is a 140,000-square-foot sheet-metal mass in gold, silver, deep red, blue and purple, with the Seattle Center Monorail passing right through it. Seattle never settled its opinion: a New York Times critic likened it to something that crawled out of the sea and died, and Forbes put it among the world's ugliest buildings, while others call it a fitting home for rock memorabilia. The central hall, the Sky Church, is a nod to Hendrix and a concert room for up to 800 people under one of the largest indoor LED screens in the world.

Galleries cover fantasy, science fiction, horror film, indie video games and African American music, and they rotate, so check what is currently up. The Science Fiction and Fantasy Hall of Fame lives here too, with members ranging from Ursula K. Le Guin to Star Wars. In Sound Lab you can play real instruments, and the On Stage gallery lets you perform in front of a virtual crowd. Don't miss IF VI WAS IX, a towering sculpture built from more than 500 instruments and 30 computers that you can listen to through headphones.
For the photo most people come for, catch a monorail train as it slides through the building.
Put on the headphones at IF VI WAS IX to hear the different musical combinations it plays.
The Space Needle, downtown and Mount Rainier, all in one frame.

Kerry Park is a sliver of lawn, just over an acre, on the south slope of Queen Anne Hill, with a railing and a row of benches turned toward downtown Seattle. It is widely regarded as the classic view of the city: the Space Needle sits in the middle, Elliott Bay spreads out to the west, and on a clear day Mount Rainier rises behind the towers. The panorama also takes in the West Seattle peninsula and Bainbridge Island. You have probably seen it already, because TV news uses it as Seattle's backdrop, it appears in the opening credits of 10 Things I Hate About You, and it served as the view from Frasier's apartment.

The land was a gift. Albert S. Kerry, a lumberman and businessman, and his wife Katharine lived nearby and gave it to the city in 1927 so that anyone passing could enjoy the view. In 1971 their children paid for the park's centerpiece, Changing Form, a hollow steel sculpture by Doris Totten Chase that stands about 15 feet tall. Children climb through it, and photographers use its curves to frame the skyline.

There isn't much to do here beyond looking, and that is the reason to come. On clear evenings the railing fills with people photographing the city. A stairway at the west end leads down to Bayview-Kinnear Park, which has a small playground.
Shoot through the openings in the Changing Form sculpture to frame the skyline.
Come on a clear day if you want Mount Rainier in the picture, and expect crowds on clear evenings.
Seattle's westernmost point: a lighthouse, two beaches, and an old fort.

Discovery Park covers 534 acres on the Magnolia peninsula and is the largest public park in Seattle. Forest, open prairie, sandy beaches and high bluffs above Puget Sound all fit inside it, laced with nearly 12 miles of walking trails. The West Point Lighthouse stands at its tip, the farthest west you can go in the city, and the Daybreak Star Cultural Center also sits within the park's boundaries.

The land was once the Army's Fort Lawton, which the city handed over in 1898. The fort opened in 1900. In 1938 the Army offered it back for a dollar, and Seattle declined because it worried about upkeep. Surplus acreage finally came to the city in the early 1970s, and the park was dedicated in 1973. Its name honors HMS Discovery, the ship George Vancouver sailed when he made the first European survey of Puget Sound in 1792. The remaining fort was formally closed in 2012. Both the Fort Lawton Historic District and the lighthouse are on the National Register of Historic Places, and some of the old buildings still stand, partly decaying, around the main lawn.

Most visitors walk the 2.8-mile Loop Trail, a National Recreation Trail that circles the upland through woods, meadow and scrub and opens onto views of the Sound. Paths branch off to the shore. South Beach faces the wind over Elliott Bay, and North Beach lies on the sheltered side toward Shilshole Bay. This is one of Seattle's best places to watch wildlife: around 270 bird species have been recorded here and in the nearby waters, harbor seals and California sea lions use the bays, and Townsend's chipmunks live in the woods.
Save some energy for the end if you walk down to North Beach, because the climb back up is moderately steep.
Head to the large meadow on the south bluff for wide views over the water; Mount Rainier can be seen from the park.
Rusting gas-plant towers turned into Seattle's strangest, most-loved lawn.

On a grassy point jutting into the north shore of Lake Union, the towers, pipes and tanks of an old coal-gas plant still stand, rusted and fenced, in the middle of a public park. The plant made gas for Seattle from 1906 until the city switched to natural gas in 1956. It is the last surviving coal gasification plant in the United States, and the park is listed on the National Register of Historic Places. A Seattle Times-affiliated site once called it easily the strangest park in the city.

The city bought the site in 1962. Landscape architect Richard Haag set up an office on the grounds, decided the machinery was worth keeping, and persuaded a doubtful public to agree. His design opened in 1975 and won a national design award. It was among the first parks to treat industrial ruins as something to celebrate, a shift Paul Goldberger praised in the New York Times. Not everyone agreed: councilwoman Myrtle Edwards had led the campaign to acquire the land, and her family asked for her name to be taken off the park because the plant was kept. The contaminated soil was treated with sludge and sawdust to grow the lawns.

The Great Mound, an artificial hill built from foundation rubble, is the place for flying kites and for looking across the water to downtown. At its top is a mosaic sundial in which your own shadow tells the time. Below it, the tallest generator towers reach 80 feet. The old pump house is now a play barn with its compressors and piping still inside, and the boiler house serves as a picnic shelter. The 1936 coal-unloading prow juts into the lake. The park has appeared in Singles and 10 Things I Hate About You.
Climb the Great Mound for the park's widest view of the towers, the lake and downtown.
Stay off the towers: there have been repeated serious and fatal falls from them.
Follow the Hammering Man's swinging arm into Seattle's main art collection.

The Seattle Art Museum, known locally as SAM, is the city's principal art museum. Its downtown home on First Avenue holds roughly 25,000 works that range across Europe, Asia, Africa, the Northwest Coast and contemporary art. The institution also runs the Seattle Asian Art Museum in Volunteer Park and the free Olympic Sculpture Park on the waterfront.

SAM opened in 1933 in an Art Deco building on Capitol Hill. Richard Fuller and his mother paid for it in the depths of the Depression, and Fuller went on to direct the museum into the 1970s without ever drawing a salary. In 1991 the collection moved downtown to a limestone building by Robert Venturi and Denise Scott Brown, trimmed with bands of tile and terra cotta. A 2007 expansion into the lower floors of an adjoining tower by Brad Cloepfil added 70 percent more gallery space. In 1999 the museum returned a Matisse odalisque looted by the Nazis to the heirs of the dealer Paul Rosenberg, one of the earliest such restitutions by an American museum.

Jonathan Borofsky's towering Hammering Man stands outside the entrance. It toppled during its first installation attempt in 1991 and went up the following year. Highlights in the galleries include Lucas Cranach the Elder's Judgment of Paris, Mark Tobey's Electric Night, a Tlingit Raven Screen from about 1810, Do-Ho Suh's Some/One, and Kane Quaye's coffin shaped like a Mercedes-Benz.
The grand main staircase from the Venturi building, called the Art Ladder, is open to the public without a ticket.
Symphony light-rail station is the closest transit stop.
Calder, Serra and Bourgeois on a reclaimed oil site above Puget Sound.

This free outdoor sculpture park, run by the Seattle Art Museum, covers about nine acres at the north end of Seattle's Central Waterfront in Belltown. It combines open-air galleries of modern and contemporary sculpture, an indoor pavilion and a stretch of beach on Puget Sound, and it is one of the few green spaces in downtown Seattle. Along with its permanent collection it shows temporary and site-specific works, and the museum rotates a major installation through it.

The ground was once industrial. Unocal ran an oil and gas operation here until the 1970s, and the site sat as a contaminated brownfield until the museum proposed turning it into a home for large sculpture. The New York firm Weiss/Manfredi designed the park, which opened in 2007, and Mary and Jon Shirley gave $30 million to found it. The project also rebuilt about 1,000 feet of seawall and shoreline next door, where a stepped slope of rock was built to recreate intertidal habitat for juvenile salmon. The park did cost something: the historic Waterfront Streetcar lost its maintenance barn to it and stopped running in 2005.

The collection includes Alexander Calder's red steel Eagle, Richard Serra's rust-colored Corten steel Wake, Jaume Plensa's large white head Echo, and Louise Bourgeois's Father and Son fountain and her Eye Benches, which you can sit on. There is also Mark di Suvero's timber-and-steel Bunyon's Chess, Roxy Paine's stainless-steel tree Split, Tony Smith's Stinger and Wandering Rocks, and Mark Dion's Neukom Vivarium, a fallen nurse log kept in its own greenhouse.
Look but don't touch: hand oils damage surfaces such as the delicate rust patina on Serra's Wake.
Bourgeois's Eye Benches are both artwork and seating, so they make a good place to rest while you look out over the Sound.
Sit inside a glass dome while Puget Sound's sharks and salmon circle overhead.

Set on Piers 59 and 60 along the Elliott Bay waterfront, the Seattle Aquarium is mostly about the waters right outside its door: the cold, rich coastal sea of Puget Sound and the Washington coast. A third building, the Ocean Pavilion, opened in 2024 and turns the focus to the tropical Coral Triangle near Indonesia. It is clad in yellow cedar meant to evoke driftwood and carries artwork by Lummi artist Dan Friday. An overpass links the waterfront promenade with Pike Place Market.

Voters approved a city aquarium in a 1968 bond measure. A first site near Golden Gardens in Ballard was dropped after public outcry, and the aquarium finally opened on the downtown piers in 1977. Salmon fingerlings were released into the bay as part of the opening ceremonies. Local scientists, including future governor Dixy Lee Ray, helped shape the exhibits. A nonprofit society has run the aquarium since 2010 and works on species recovery, such as rearing endangered pinto abalone and helping restore leopard sharks in Indonesia.

The centerpiece is the Underwater Dome, built with the original aquarium: a near-spherical glass room set inside a 400,000-gallon tank full of lingcod, sturgeon, skates, rockfish and sharks. Pier 60 also has harbor seals, fur seals, sea and river otters, and an open-air cliff habitat for tufted puffins and murres. On Pier 59 you'll find a giant Pacific octopus in a round tank, a ring of moon jellies, a wave tank and touch pools with sea stars and urchins. The Ocean Pavilion's Reef habitat gives a large window onto sharks, rays and schooling tropical fish.
Catch a dive show at Window on Washington Waters, where divers in special masks talk with visitors from inside the tank.
Look for the window into the veterinary clinic on Pier 60, where you can sometimes watch staff examine animals.
Rem Koolhaas's glass-and-steel library, where nonfiction climbs four floors in one ramp.

Seattle's flagship public library opened in 2004 in the downtown core. It is an 11-story building of glass and steel, designed by Rem Koolhaas and Joshua Prince-Ramus of the Dutch firm OMA with Seattle's LMN Architects. From the street it reads as a set of stacked, offset platforms held inside a diagonal steel mesh, with nearly 10,000 custom-made windows. Its designers set out to celebrate the printed book and to make a library feel inviting rather than stuffy, and they let the building's functions decide its shape. In its first year it drew 2.3 million visitors, about 30% of them from outside the city.

This is the third central library on the same block between Fourth and Fifth Avenues, after a 1906 Beaux-Arts Carnegie library and a 1960 International Style building. Voters funded the current one in 1998, and Bill Gates added $20 million. Critics have disagreed about the result ever since. The New Yorker's Paul Goldberger called it the most exhilarating new library in a generation. A Seattle critic later called it oppressive and confusing, and its layout has become a case study in how people find their way through complex buildings.

From the Fourth Avenue lobby, an escalator rises to the Living Room on level three, which has a café and gift shop. Level four is the Red Floor, finished in 13 shades of red. The Books Spiral carries the nonfiction collection up levels six through nine on one gently sloping, continuous run of shelves, so the Dewey sequence never breaks. Level nine holds the map room and genealogy collection. Level ten has the Seattle Room for local history, a 400-seat reading room and the highest viewpoints in the building. George Tsutakawa's "Fountain of Wisdom", saved from the 1960 library, now stands on the Fourth Avenue side.
Go up to level ten for the building's highest views and the large reading room.
Walk the Books Spiral from level six to nine to follow the whole nonfiction collection in one continuous climb.
An 18-foot concrete troll crushing a real Volkswagen Beetle under a bridge.

The Fremont Troll crouches beneath the north end of the Aurora Bridge (formally the George Washington Memorial Bridge), at N. 36th Street and Troll Avenue N. in Seattle's Fremont neighborhood. Built of steel rebar, wire and concrete, it stands 18 feet tall and weighs about 13,000 pounds. One hand grips a genuine Volkswagen Beetle with California plates, as though the troll had just plucked it off the roadway overhead. The idea comes from the Scandinavian folk tale of a troll that lives under a bridge.

In 1990 the Fremont Arts Council held a competition for the space under the bridge. Locals wanted a piece of art there in place of the trash and people sleeping rough, and the troll won easily. Steve Badanes, Will Martin, Donna Walter and Ross Whitehead sculpted it, and it went up that same year. Part of what drew neighbors to this odd design was unease about large apartment and office developments arriving in the mostly residential area. The Beetle once held a time capsule containing a plaster bust of Elvis, which was stolen by vandals. Graffiti has been a recurring problem since, and volunteers clean it off regularly. In 2005 the stretch of road running downhill from the troll to N. 34th Street was renamed Troll Avenue.

Most visitors come to climb on it and take photos, as characters do in the film 10 Things I Hate About You and the video game Life Is Strange. A rebuilt stairway leads up to the top of the sculpture, and volunteers have added plantings around it.
Use the stairway beside the sculpture to climb up for a view of the troll from above.
Look closely at the crushed Beetle in the troll's hand, which still carries its California license plate.
Where zoos first tried hiding the bars inside a jungle.

Woodland Park Zoo sits on the western half of Woodland Park in Seattle's Phinney Ridge neighborhood. Around 900 animals of roughly 250 species live across its grounds, which are as much garden as zoo, with thousands of trees and over a thousand plant species. It has won more Best National Exhibit awards from the Association of Zoos and Aquariums than any US zoo except the Bronx Zoo.

The zoo grew out of a small menagerie on the estate of lumberman and developer Guy Phinney. After his death, his widow sold the land to the city in 1899, at a price so steep the mayor vetoed the deal before the council overruled him. The Olmsted Brothers later laid out the park. Its biggest mark on the wider world came in the late 1970s. Director David Hancocks rebuilt the gorilla enclosure so that animals and visitors shared the same planted, rocky, acoustically softened landscape. Experts doubted that the plants would survive or that visitors would see anything. The design became known as the landscape immersion exhibit and was copied by zoos worldwide. Decades earlier, a gorilla named Bobo had been one of Seattle's biggest attractions.

Tropical Asia is the largest section, with an Indian rhino reserve, Malayan tigers and sloth bears in Banyan Wilds, and orangutans and siamangs along the Trail of Vines. The African Savanna mixes giraffes, zebras and ostriches, with lions and hyenas nearby. The Living Northwest Trail, modeled on a trail in Denali, has grizzlies, wolves, elk and mountain goats. Tropical Rain Forest holds the gorillas, lemurs and a jaguar. Temperate Forest has red pandas, cranes, flamingos and a petting farm. Families also head for the Zoomazium indoor play space and a 1918 Philadelphia Toboggan Company carousel, first built for the Cincinnati Zoo.
See the western lowland gorillas in Tropical Rain Forest, the descendants of the exhibit that launched immersion design.
At the Humboldt penguin habitat, look for the underwater viewing windows.
Seattle's gayborhood, coffee laboratory and late-night district on one steep hill.

Capitol Hill rises steeply just east of downtown, across I-5, and is one of Seattle's most crowded residential districts as well as its main nightlife quarter. Broadway is the commercial spine, while the Pike-Pine corridor packs coffeehouses, bars, restaurants and music venues into mid-rise buildings, many of them former car showrooms from the early 1900s, when this was the city's auto row. Farther north and east the mood changes: 14th Avenue E. below Volunteer Park was once called Millionaire's Row, and historic mansions sometimes stand right beside plain studio apartment blocks.

From the 1960s, cheap rents in the emptying auto row drew artists and LGBTQ residents leaving a declining Pioneer Square, and the Hill has been Seattle's gay village ever since. Pride parades were held here for decades, and the neighborhood was hit hard by the AIDS epidemic. Cal Anderson Park is named for Washington's first openly gay legislator, who died in 1995, and the AIDS Memorial Pathway, an outdoor art installation, sits on the plaza above the light rail station. Since the 2010s, rapid construction and rising rents have pushed many longtime residents elsewhere.

Come in the evening for live music, fringe theater and bars. The Egyptian Theatre, set in a former Masonic lodge, and the Northwest Film Forum both screen festival films. Espresso Vivace on Broadway is credited with starting artisanal coffee and latte art in the US. Look out for the rainbow crosswalks along Pike-Pine, and walk up to Volunteer Park, where the water tower stands at the Hill's highest point.
The light rail station on Broadway puts you right beside Cal Anderson Park and the AIDS Memorial Pathway.
For the area's grandest houses, walk 14th Avenue E. just south of Volunteer Park.
Watch scientists at work behind glass beside a world-class T. rex skull.

The Burke is the University of Washington's natural history museum, the oldest museum in the state and Washington's official state museum. It holds more than 16 million objects and specimens across anthropology, biology and geology, among them the world's largest collection of spread bird wings and a Northwest Coast collection the museum ranks as the fifth largest holding of Native American art anywhere.

It started in 1879 as a naturalist club of Seattle high school students, which grew into the region's largest natural history collection once a biology instructor nicknamed "Bug" Johnson arrived with 20,000 specimens. The state designated it the Washington State Museum in 1899. It then moved through a string of leftover 1909 exposition buildings, one leaky and one infested with bark beetles. A bequest from Caroline McGilvra Burke, given in her late husband's memory, helped fund a 1964 building that carried his name. That building was replaced in 2019 by a new one designed by Tom Kundig.

The new building's big draw is its windows into working research areas, which put normally hidden collections and the people studying them on view. The permanent galleries include Fossils Uncovered, with one of the best-preserved T. rex skulls in the world, plus Northwest Native Art, Culture is Living, Amazing Life and Our Material World. A Baird's beaked whale skeleton, from an animal that washed up on a Washington beach in 2015, hangs in the lobby. Outside are totem poles and a garden of about 60 Washington-native plant species, and the Off the Rez café serves Native American food, frybread included.
Make time for Fossils Uncovered and its T. rex skull, one of the best preserved anywhere.
Look into the glass-walled research spaces, where scientists work with collections that were never shown before.
Seattle's 1914 skyscraper, with a 35th-floor observatory and a legendary wishing chair.

Finished in 1914 in Pioneer Square, this 38-story, 462-foot tower was among the tallest buildings outside New York when it opened. It held the title of tallest building west of the Mississippi until 1931 and stayed the tallest on the West Coast until the Space Needle went up in 1962. Its granite base and white terra-cotta skin, topped by a pyramid roof, still stand out among the newer towers downtown. It became a Seattle landmark in 1984.

The money came from Lyman Cornelius Smith, a Syracuse typewriter and firearms industrialist who was once Seattle's biggest taxpayer. He first planned a modest 14-story building. His son Burns persuaded him to go much higher and take the record from rival Tacoma. The elder Smith died in 1910 before ground was broken, so Burns oversaw the job. Even before the building was finished, its image was being sent out nationwide to sell Seattle as a rising city. On opening day, July 4, 1914, more than 4,000 people rode up to the 35th floor. The tower later had a string of owners, including restaurateur Ivar Haglund, who bought it in 1976.

Today's visitors go up to the 35th-floor observatory, which has an open-air walkway with views on all four sides and a bar serving vintage-style cocktails. The room is known for its carved teak ceiling and blackwood furniture, said to be a gift from China's Empress Dowager Cixi. The best-known piece is the Wishing Chair, carved with a dragon and a phoenix. Legend says any unmarried person who sits in it will marry within a year, and Smith's own daughter was married in this room. The ride up uses the building's original elevators, and the basement served as a speakeasy during Prohibition. Guided tours tell the building's history.
Look for the carved Wishing Chair in the observatory room before heading out to the views.
Take the guided tour for the building's backstory; the observatory is included.
Where Seattle began, before its founders sailed off to somewhere better.

Alki Point is the westernmost tip of West Seattle, a point pushing into Puget Sound that marks the southern edge of Elliott Bay. The neighborhood that wraps around it feels like a Pacific Northwest beach town: mid-century bungalows, waterfront apartments, cafes and a narrow beach, with a road and a bike-and-foot trail running for miles along the shore. Before settlers arrived, the Duwamish people gathered and cultivated food on nearby prairies they kept open with seasonal burning; their name for the place means "prairie point."

The Denny Party came ashore here on November 13, 1851, and laid out a settlement they called New York Alki, from a Chinook Jargon word meaning "by and by." It didn't last long. By the following spring Arthur Denny had moved to a better site across the bay, today's Pioneer Square, and most of the others eventually followed him. Well into the 20th century Alki could be reached from most of Seattle only by boat. A small hill just inland from the point is one of the city's rare bedrock outcrops, sandstone some 23 million years old that may once have stood offshore as a sea stack.

Most visitors come for Alki Beach, which looks across to the Olympic Mountains and downtown Seattle; the water is too cold for most swimmers. Along the shore you'll find the 1905 Birthplace of Seattle monument listing the first colonists, which also pays tribute to the Duwamish, and a small Statue of Liberty replica from 1952 that nods to the settlement's original name. The working 1913 Alki Point Lighthouse stands at the point, and the flower-covered holdout houses wedged between the beachfront condos are worth a look. Nearby Schmitz Park holds some of Seattle's few remaining stands of old-growth forest.
Walk or bike the shoreline trail for views across to Blake Island.
For a view over Elliott Bay from above the beach, go up to Hamilton Viewpoint Park on California Avenue SW.

plans.title: 3 days in Seattle
plans.traveler: a first visit: someone who hasn't been before and wants the places the city is known for, at an easy pace

days.intro: This day moves from the Pike Place Market's farm stalls down to the Seattle waterfront aquarium, then underground through the old streets and back up to the library and Smith Tower. It is a walking day through the city's oldest and newest sides.

stories.headline: Three Days in Seattle, From Market Stalls to Hilltop Evenings
stories.dek: For first-timers with three days, a plan that walks downtown, circles Seattle Center and then heads out to the parks, locks and Capitol Hill, with the views saved for the right light.
intro: These three days move outward from the water. The first stays downtown and on foot: the market in the morning, the aquarium on the piers, the streets the city buried after its great fire, a library that still divides critics, and a 1914 tower for the evening light. The second circles Seattle Center, from blown glass and Gehry's guitar-inspired museum down to a sculpture park by the bay and back up the Needle.

The third goes farther afield, to a park on the city's westernmost point, the locks where boats and salmon pass between lake and sea, a troll, a rusting gas plant, and a long evening on Capitol Hill. Along the way, Seattle keeps showing itself to you from above.

days.heading: Market, waterfront and the buried city

parts.text: The first morning begins where Seattle has been buying its food since 1907, at the market its voters once saved from demolition. Come early, while the fishmongers and flower sellers set the tone, and don't stay only on the upper arcade: the levels below hold antique dealers, comic shops and small family restaurants.

Have lunch nearby, then cross the overpass to the waterfront promenade; the aquarium is only a few minutes' walk from the market. Make for the Underwater Dome, a glass room set inside a huge tank where sharks, sturgeon and rockfish move past on every side, and see whether a dive show is on at Window on Washington Waters.

From the piers, walk into Pioneer Square for the afternoon's odd turn underground. After the fire of 1889 the city raised its streets by as much as a full story, and on a guided tour you walk the old sidewalks left beneath them, looking up at glass vault lights, now tinted amethyst, set into the pavement overhead.

Back in daylight, a short walk brings you to the library, a very different idea of the city. Ride up to the Living Room, follow the Books Spiral as it carries the whole nonfiction collection up four floors without a break, and finish on level ten for the building's highest views.

Smith Tower is saved for last, as the light begins to soften. The original elevators take you up to the 35th-floor observatory, where the carved Wishing Chair waits inside before you step out onto the open-air walkway that runs around all four sides.
Dinner is close by, so the day ends without a trek: a market, a buried street, a library and a 1914 skyscraper, all of it on foot.

Seattle Center fills up as the day goes on, so start with the glass while it is still quiet. Move through the galleries to the Glasshouse, where a single suspended sculpture about 100 feet long hangs in reds, oranges and yellows, and if the Hot Shop is working, stop to watch local artists shape molten glass.

After lunch nearby, MOPOP is only a few minutes' walk away and gets the longest stretch of the day. Frank Gehry worked from Fender Stratocasters for its sheet-metal shell; inside, the galleries rotate, but put on the headphones at IF VI WAS IX, a tower built from more than 500 instruments, and watch for the monorail sliding straight through the building.

By mid-afternoon, walk down to the bay. The sculpture park sits on what was once an oil and gas site and now holds Calder's red Eagle and Serra's rust-colored Wake; look without touching, then rest on Louise Bourgeois's Eye Benches and gaze out over the Sound.

Walk back up to the Needle as the afternoon draws on. Give yourself a full turn on the Loupe, the revolving glass floor that lets the city pass slowly beneath your feet, and look down on the Chihuly garden you walked through this morning.

Eat near the Needle, then walk up Queen Anne Hill for the view you have probably already seen on the news. From the railing at Kerry Park the Space Needle sits in the middle of the frame with downtown and Elliott Bay around it, Mount Rainier behind on a clear evening; try framing it through the openings of the Changing Form sculpture.

days.heading: Bluffs, boats and the Hill at night

parts.text: The last day reaches beyond downtown, starting in the city's largest park, out on the Magnolia peninsula. Walk the Loop Trail through woods and meadow, stop at the big meadow on the south bluff to look out over the water, and if you take a path down to North Beach, keep something back for the climb up.

A short ride by car or bus brings you to the locks, where everything from kayaks to fishing boats back from the Bering Sea is raised or lowered between lake and sea. Go down to the fish ladder's underground room too, where in season the windows show salmon working their way upstream.

Lunch near the locks, then ride across to Fremont for a quick, silly stop. The troll under the Aurora Bridge is crushing a real Volkswagen Beetle, California plates still on it, and the stairway beside it lets you look down on him from above.

From the troll it is an easy walk to Lake Union and Gas Works Park, where the rusted towers of an old coal-gas plant stand fenced in the middle of the lawns. Climb the Great Mound for the view across the water to downtown, and find the sundial at the top, where your own shadow tells the time.

Late in the afternoon, take a car or bus to Capitol Hill and plan to stay into the evening, when the bars, music venues and theaters along Pike-Pine fill up. Stop at Espresso Vivace on Broadway, follow the rainbow crosswalks, and if your legs allow, walk up to Volunteer Park and its water tower at the top of the Hill.
Have dinner on the Hill itself. After three days of looking at Seattle from towers, bluffs and lawns, it is a good place to end up in the thick of it.

good_to_know: The Seattle Underground can only be seen on a guided tour, so check tour times and book ahead to fit the mid-afternoon slot on day one.

Days one and two are entirely on foot. Day three needs a car or bus for three legs: Discovery Park to the locks, the locks to Fremont, and Gas Works Park to Capitol Hill; the troll to Gas Works is a walk.
Each day's order is built around closing times, so check the aquarium's last entry and the hours of the library, Smith Tower, MOPOP and the Space Needle before you go.
For salmon at the locks' viewing windows, early July to mid-August is best; each lock chamber is drained for about two weeks a year, the large one usually in November and the small one in March.
Mount Rainier shows from Kerry Park and Discovery Park only on clear days, and Kerry Park's railing gets crowded on clear evenings. MOPOP's galleries rotate, so see what is on before you go.
stories.closing: You leave having seen the Space Needle from its own glass floor and from Kerry Park's railing, with a buried sidewalk under Pioneer Square to tell people about at home.
